questions.prompt: Starting from items = [], a click queues [A], then its timer calls setItems(items.map(...)). What array does that captured map read?

options.label: The empty array from the render that created the handler.
The latest committed array, because the timer runs later.
A Promise that resolves to the next state.

questions.explanation: The callback keeps the render’s empty array, so mapping it returns []. A later timer does not refresh a closure. useState supplies a value and a setter; neither the captured array nor the setter result is a Promise for future state.

questions.prompt: Which change preserves independently added items when asynchronous completions arrive out of order?

options.label: Use functional updates for both appending and updating the matching item ID.
Fix only the append, then replace the array captured by each callback.
Make the timeout long enough for every render to finish.

questions.explanation: Each dependent write must build on pending state, and each completion must target its own item ID. A later stale replacement can undo a correct append. Waiting longer does not change the captured array or establish an ordering policy.

questions.prompt: Why does await setItems(next) fail to make the old handler read the new items value?

options.label: The setter does not return a commit Promise, and this handler keeps its render snapshot.
React setters cannot be called from async functions.
await freezes React rendering until the component unmounts.

questions.explanation: Calling a setter from async code is valid. Its return value is not a Promise that waits for a commit, and await does not replace the handler’s captured variables. It also does not freeze React rendering; calculate dependent state with a pure updater.

questions.prompt: Where should a request run when its result updates an item?

options.label: Outside the state updater; await it, then queue a pure update by ID.
Inside an async updater passed to setItems.
Inside a synchronous updater so it runs exactly once.

questions.explanation: Perform I/O outside the updater, then calculate the next state synchronously. An async updater returns a Promise instead of an array. A synchronous updater with I/O is still impure: development Strict Mode can invoke updaters twice, so it cannot promise one request.

questions.prompt: Two requests edit the same item. The newer result arrives first. Do functional updates alone stop the older response from overwriting it?

options.label: No. Use a per-item request revision or serialize writes according to the chosen policy.
Yes. Functional updates sort responses by request start time.
Yes. Using an item ID makes every response for that ID current.

questions.explanation: Functional updates receive pending state but do not infer which request is authoritative. Responses are not sorted by start time. An item ID identifies the target; a request revision distinguishes competing operations for that target.

questions.prompt: A timeout has already started awaiting a request when Clear items is clicked. What prevents its late response from affecting a new list?

options.label: Invalidate its generation and check that generation before applying the result.
Only call clearTimeout on the timer that already fired.
Assume aborting the client request rolls back any server write.

questions.explanation: A generation guard rejects the old operation’s result locally. clearTimeout cannot stop an already-running callback. Abort can reduce unnecessary work when supported, but it is not proof that the server rolled back or never committed a mutation.
